title: BRUTAL framework
by: Ahwoo Ltd (RocketWerkz, the studio of DayZ creator Dean Hall)
what: The free toolkit that RimWorld's new engine is built on. Game makers can use it for free. They must show its logo and credits.
why: The makers said: "You are only as independent as your tools are." They want small studios to own their tools.
howToPlay: This is a tool for making games, not a game.
Ask your AI helper to read its README with you if you want to try it.

title: Worlds Upon the Wind
what: A card game made in the free Godot engine. The code and art were given to everyone. The music and sounds were not, because of other people's rights.
why: The developer wanted to give other indie game makers a real, finished game to learn from, and to give back.
howToPlay: Install Godot 4.7 (free) from godotengine.org.
Download the code from GitHub (green "Code" button, then "Download ZIP").
Open the folder in Godot and press Play. Or buy it on Steam to support the developer.

title: Unturned (U3 SDK)
license: Custom: free mods only, no selling
what: The code for the free zombie survival game, shared on its 12th birthday. Great for learning and making mods. You can't sell what you make.
why: So players can build "a lasting legacy" for the game, whatever happens to it later. They hope to switch to the MIT license one day.
howToPlay: Install Unturned on Steam. It is free.
The code uses the files from your Steam copy.
Mods you make must be free.

title: Carbon engine (EVE Online)
by: Fenris Creations (the new name of CCP Games)
what: The engine behind the space game EVE Online, now free for anyone to use. The game itself is not included.
why: To make the base of their games "visible, understandable, and useful to others", and to work together with the community.
howToPlay: This is a tool for making games, not a game.
Each part has its own folder on GitHub with a README.

title: Arma: Cold War Assault Remastered
what: A remastered army game from 2001, shared for its 25th birthday. The code is open. The free demo gives you game files to play with.
why: So the fans who kept the game alive for 25 years can study it, fix it, and build new things.
howToPlay: Get the free demo on Steam for the game files.
Build the code from GitHub with your AI helper, or just play the demo.

title: Moon Child (1997)
by: Its original makers: Reinier van Vliet, Metin Seven and Ramon Braumuller
what: A classic jump-and-run game from 1997. The team shared the code and the art after the game went viral online. The art is for non-commercial use.
why: Fans fell in love with it again, so the original team released it for everyone to enjoy and port.
howToPlay: Get it free from the makers' itch.io page.
Or try a fan-made modern version, like Moon Child SR on GitHub.

title: COCOS 4 engine
what: A popular engine for phone and web games. It became fully free, with all the business limits removed.
why: The new owner removed the commercial limits so more people can use it and help improve it.
howToPlay: This is a tool for making games, not a game.

title: s&box
by: Facepunch (the makers of Garry's Mod and Rust)
license: MIT (some files under its own EULA)
what: The code for s&box, a game-making sandbox from the makers of Garry's Mod. A few built files keep their own rules.
why: So players and creators can see how it works and help build it.
howToPlay: This is mostly a tool for making games and mods.

title: Zork I, II and III
what: Some of the first adventure games ever, from 1980. You play by typing, like "go north". The code is the whole game, so it is all free now.
why: So students, teachers and game makers can study, learn and play. They worked with the Internet Archive to save it.
howToPlay: The code is on GitHub (zork1, zork2 and zork3).
Ask your AI helper to build it with the free ZILF tool and play it in a free story-game app.

title: Command & Conquer (4 classic games)
what: The code for Tiberian Dawn, Red Alert, Renegade, and Generals with Zero Hour. The art, music and movies are still EA's, so you need your own copy.
why: To let fans fix and mod these classic games more deeply. EA added new modding tools and Steam Workshop at the same time.
howToPlay: Own the game (the Command & Conquer Ultimate Collection on Steam or the EA app).
Easiest: play Generals with the fan-made GeneralsGameCode builds, or Red Alert with OpenRA.

title: Duelyst
what: A card battle game that shut down in 2020. Its code and over 600 animated pictures were given to everyone, so fans can run it again.
why: The servers were turned off. Sharing everything was the only way to keep the game alive.
howToPlay: Look for fan-run servers on the project's GitHub page.

title: Quake
what: The engine of the famous 1996 shooter. The levels, art and sounds are still owned by the company.
why: id Software shared its old engines so people could learn from them and keep them running.
howToPlay: Use your own copy of Quake, or the free LibreQuake game files.
Play with a modern free engine like vkQuake or Ironwail.

title: Doom
what: The code of the 1993 classic. It was shared in 1997 and became fully open in 1999. The levels and art are still owned by the company.
why: id Software wanted people to learn from it. Fans have kept Doom alive for over 30 years.
howToPlay: Use your own copy of Doom, or the free Freedoom game files.
Play with a free modern engine like UZDoom.
